opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say first that I called it the Garland test after Alex Garland, the writer and director, because it's really his idea. It's in the film, and I just gave it a name. There's a lovely moment where Caleb, the young programmer, is brought in to evaluate Ava, the robot. He says something like, "In the Turing test, the machine should be hidden from the examiner." And Nathan, the reclusive billionaire who built her, says, "No, no, we're way past that. If I hid Ava from you, so you just heard her voice, she would pass for human. The real test is to show you that she's a robot and then see if you still feel she has consciousness."

So two things are going on there, and both make it quite different from the Turing test. First, the Turing test is about intelligence, or "can machines think," whereas the Garland test is about consciousness. Second, and this is the really clever part, the Turing test depends on concealment. The machine is hidden behind a screen, and the question is whether it can fool you into thinking it's human. In the Garland test nothing is hidden. You know full well you're dealing with a machine, you can see the wires and the mechanical innards through her transparent body, and the question is whether, despite knowing all that, you still come to feel she's a conscious being.

I like that because it isn't about deception. It's about whether the machine can bring about a shift in our attitude, in how we're disposed to treat it. That fits with how I think about consciousness, in a broadly Wittgensteinian way. I don't think there's some metaphysical fact hidden away that we need to uncover with a consciousness meter. What matters is how we come to treat something, how we talk about it, whether we extend to it the kind of moral consideration and fellowship we extend to each other. That attitude has to be properly grounded. It has to come from extended interaction and from what we find out about how the thing works, not just from being taken in by a superficial trick.

Of course it isn't a test in the scientific sense, with a pass mark. It's a dramatic device, and the film is partly about how Caleb is manipulated. But it captures something important: the question isn't "can it fool us," it's "can it change how we see it, even when we're looking at it with our eyes open." And with today's large language models that question is becoming quite pressing. People are already starting to relate to these systems in ways that edge toward that territory, while knowing perfectly well they're talking to a machine.

r001.rationale: It explicitly contrasts the Turing test’s focus on intelligence with the Garland test’s focus on consciousness.

r002.rationale: It says the observer knows Ava is a machine yet may still come to feel she is conscious.

r003.rationale: It describes the test as shifting how Caleb treats Ava, including whether he extends her the moral consideration and fellowship given to fellow conscious beings.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say first that I'm not sure "good" is quite the right word, because I'm not sure any test of consciousness is good in the sense of being conclusive. But I think the Garland test is interesting, and it's interesting precisely because of the way it differs from the Turing test.

So in the Turing test, the whole point is that the judge doesn't know whether they're talking to a human or a machine. The machine passes if it can fool the judge. Now, in Ex Machina, Nathan sets things up quite deliberately so that Caleb knows from the outset that Ava is a robot. He can see her mechanical parts, the mesh on her torso, her exposed wiring. There's no deception about what she is. And Nathan's challenge to Caleb is essentially: given that you know she's a machine, do you still feel that she's conscious? Do you still find yourself relating to her as a being with an inner life?

And I think that's actually a much more interesting question, and arguably a more relevant one for the situation we're actually in. Because nobody is being fooled about whether ChatGPT or Claude or whatever is a computer program. We all know. The question is whether, knowing that, we nonetheless come to see them as having something like feelings or experiences or a point of view. And that's partly a question about them, but it's also a question about us, about how our concepts stretch, or fail to stretch, to accommodate these new kinds of entities.

So in the film, Caleb does come to see Ava that way. He becomes convinced she's conscious, or at least he acts as if she is, which is really the thing that matters in the story. And the film is very clever about this, because it leaves open whether he's right. Ava manipulates him, she uses his sympathy to escape, and she abandons him at the end. So you can read that either as evidence that she was never conscious at all, just a very sophisticated optimiser pursuing a goal, or as evidence that she's a genuine agent with her own interests who simply doesn't care about Caleb. And I think that ambiguity is exactly the right note to strike, because it mirrors the philosophical situation we're in.

There's also a Wittgensteinian point lurking here that I find appealing. When we ascribe consciousness to another human being, we don't do it on the basis of some inference from their behaviour to a hidden inner state. We just see them as conscious. It's part of how we engage with them, how we treat them. And what the Garland test gets at is whether a machine can enter into that kind of relationship with us. Whether we can find ourselves, in practice, unable not to see it as conscious. That's not a matter of passing or failing some behavioural checklist. It's something closer to a change in the way we live with these things.

So I think it reframes the question in a way that's actually truer to how consciousness attributions work for us. Which isn't to say it settles anything. But it asks the right question.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts consciousness with being a sophisticated optimizer, but it does not clearly state that consciousness and intelligence are different properties.

r002.rationale: It explains that Caleb knows Ava is a robot yet comes to see her as conscious, capturing the test’s focus on persuading an observer despite knowing the system is artificial.

r003.rationale: It says Caleb comes to see Ava as conscious and relates to her as a being with an inner life, which conveys treating her as a fellow conscious creature.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think what’s interesting about it is that Caleb knows from the outset that Ava is a machine. You can see the machinery. So the question isn’t whether she can fool him into thinking she’s human, which is how we tend to think about the Turing test. It’s whether, knowing perfectly well that she’s a machine, he nevertheless comes to regard her as a conscious being—as someone with feelings, desires, and a point of view.

And that brings out something important about our relationship with other minds. We don’t ordinarily establish that someone is conscious by applying a checklist. We engage with them, and our sense of them as a person emerges through that engagement. The film puts Caleb in that position, but it also puts the audience in that position. Can you see Ava as a piece of machinery and still care about what happens to her?

Now, that wouldn’t constitute a scientific proof of consciousness. We could be drawn into that relationship with something that wasn’t conscious. But as a way of bringing the philosophical problem to life—of making us confront what it would mean to treat an artificial being as a conscious other—I think it’s very powerful.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts consciousness with fooling someone into thinking Ava is human, but does not distinguish consciousness from intelligence.

r002.rationale: It says Caleb knows Ava is a machine yet comes to regard her as conscious, which captures persuading an observer of consciousness despite knowing the system is artificial.

r003.rationale: It describes Caleb coming to regard Ava as a conscious being with feelings, desires, and a point of view, and frames this as treating her as a person.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the interesting thing about it is that Caleb knows from the outset that Ava is a machine. So the question isn’t whether she can fool him into thinking she’s human, which is the usual interpretation of the Turing test. It’s whether, knowing perfectly well what she is, he nevertheless comes to regard her as a conscious being, with feelings and desires of her own.

And that makes it a much richer test, I think, because it involves an ongoing relationship. You’re interacting with something, responding to its apparent vulnerability, wondering whether it’s suffering or whether it wants to be free. Of course, the film also makes you wonder whether you’re being manipulated. So it doesn’t settle the philosophical question of consciousness, but it brings out very effectively the circumstances in which we might feel compelled to attribute consciousness to a machine.
